questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman presented with vaginal discharge and odor for one week. She was sexually active with one regular male partner. She reported inconsistent condom use. On pelvic examination, there were no external skin lesions. A thin, white to gray vaginal discharge was present. There was no cervical discharge or cervical motion tenderness. A sample of vaginal fluid was collected. The pH of the fluid was 5.5, and a fishy odor was noted on addition of potassium hydroxide solution. On wet prep of the specimen, epithelial cell borders were obscured by bacteria. Urine NAAT for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and trichomoniasis were sent.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM plus azithromycin 1g stat

questions.explanation: Metronidazole 500 mg BD for 7 days This patient meets all four of Amsel’s criteria for bacterial vaginosis: homogeneous, thin, white discharge that smoothly coats the vaginal walls, clue cells on microscopic examination, pH of vaginal fluid of >4.5, and a fishy odor of vaginal discharge before or after addition of 10% KOH solution. Bacterial vaginosis is most commonly a polymicrobial infection related to Prevotella spp., Mobiluncus spp., or Gardnerella vaginalis. Treatment is with a 7-day course of metronidazole 500 mg BID. The 2-gram dose of metronidazole is intended for trichomoniasis therapy. Fluconazole would be appropriate for vulvovaginal candidiasis. Doxycycline and ceftriaxone are used to treat common causes of cervicitis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q20

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of smelly vaginal discharge. She was 16+2 weeks pregnant. On examination she had a thin, grey vaginal discharge with strong odor. Microscopy displayed clue cells and minimal lactobacilli. The doctor recommended treatment as this condition is associated with adverse outcomes in pregnancy.
questions.lead_in: What complication is associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: Miscarriage This patient has bacterial vaginosis (BV), given the clinical presentation of malodorous, thin discharge and microscopy results. BV is associated with preterm labor and miscarriage. Treatment is therefore advised during pregnancy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q20

questions.question: State the preferred therapy for the following genital infection.
questions.model_answer: a) Oral metronidazole 500 mg PO BID x 7 days is the primary regimen. Equally effective topical alternatives (more expensive) are 0.75% metronidazole vaginal gel or 2% clindamycin vaginal cream/100 mg clindamycin ovules; other alternatives include secnidazole 2 g PO once, tinidazole 1 g daily x 5 days (or 2 g daily x 2 days), oral clindamycin, and metronidazole 750 mg extended-release daily x 7 days. A single 2 g dose of metronidazole is less effective and is not recommended. Treat symptomatic women (symptom relief, reduced acquisition of chlamydia, gonorrhea, HIV, HSV-2, trichomoniasis); also treat before gynecologic surgery (e.g., hysterectomy), where metronidazole lowers postoperative infection. For multiple recurrences: 0.75% metronidazole gel twice weekly x 4-6 months, or monthly metronidazole 2 g with fluconazole 150 mg; refractory disease may respond to intravaginal boric acid 600 mg at bedtime. Probiotics are not supported.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort's advice to treat asymptomatic BV in high-risk pregnancy is not supported by the chapter, which states meta-analysis of 21 trials showed antibiotic treatment in pregnancy eradicated BV but did not reduce preterm delivery; Mandell supports pre-gynecologic-surgery treatment.

cohort_answer.text: Metronidazole 500mg PO BID x7 days. Can also use metronidazole applicator 5g once daily intravaginally x5 days OR clindamycin cream 2% one applicator 5g intravaginally once daily x7 days. Treat all symptomatic BV. Treat asymptomatic BV if: high risk pregnancy (hx preterm delivery), prior to IUD insertion, prior to gyne OR/abortion

parts.text: A woman with cervicitis and anaphylaxis to cephalosporins — what treatment?

parts_raw.text: Woman with cervicitis, anaphylaxis to cephalosporins.

questions.model_answer: With a true cephalosporin contraindication, use a non-cephalosporin dual regimen: azithromycin 2 g PO single dose plus either gentamicin 240 mg IM single dose or gemifloxacin 320 mg PO single dose (cure rates ~99.5–100%). Spectinomycin 2 g IM is an option for genital/rectal infection where available. Obtain a culture for susceptibility testing and a test of cure.
